record.paper_title: Open Questions about Time and Self-reference in Living Systems
record.original_question: How can a dynamic programming language or metamodel be used to generate dynamic models or programs for open-ended systems, and how can a dynamic metalanguage be developed for generating dynamic languages that themselves support open-ended self-modification?

evidence.quote:
The Banzhaf et al. [13] definition of openendedness requires that models and metamodels be dynamic, be
able to change as the system evolves in time (sec.55.5). However, conventional mathematical modelling
techniques and computer programming languages are static: they do not change, and they have no
facilities for their models to change, as the system evolves.

Developing a method for using such a
language (metamodel) to generate dynamic models (programs) of open ended systems remains an open
research topic; developing a dynamic metalanguage for generating dynamic languages even more so.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Call a formal modelling framework (a programming language, mathematical model, or metamodel) static if its syntax, semantics, and rule set are fixed once the framework is specified, so that any object expressed in it cannot alter its own description rules during execution. Call it dynamic if it provides intrinsic mechanisms by which the models, programs, or rules expressed in it can be modified at runtime as a function of the evolving state of the system being modelled. Call a system open-ended if, over time, it can produce qualitatively novel structures, behaviours, or organizational levels that are not enumerable in advance from its initial specification.

(a) Construct a dynamic programming language or dynamic metamodel L together with a generative procedure G such that, given a specification S of an open-ended system, G(S) produces a dynamic model (program) in L whose rules and state space evolve with the modelled system, and prove that the resulting model can faithfully track open-ended novelty in S in a precise sense to be made rigorous (e.g., that no fixed static model can simulate G(S) on arbitrary inputs without unbounded external reprogramming).

(b) Construct a dynamic metalanguage M, i.e., a formal system whose own syntactic and semantic rules can change at runtime, such that M itself generates dynamic languages of the type produced in (a), and these generated languages support open-ended self-modification (each generated language can, while in use, extend or revise its own syntax and semantics in response to the evolving system it models). Establish that such an M is internally consistent (free of paradox arising from self-reference at the metalevel) and characterize the class of open-ended systems for which it is adequate.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of constructing dynamic languages and especially dynamic metalanguages capable of generating models for open-ended systems is widely regarded as unresolved in the artificial life and open-endedness research community. Conventional programming languages and mathematical modelling frameworks are static, and proposals such as Banzhaf et al.'s definition of open-endedness explicitly call for dynamic models and metamodels, but no general construction is known. No published solution was located.

status_evidence.title: Defining and Simulating Open-Ended Novelty (Banzhaf et al.)
status_evidence.snippet: Argues that meaningful open-endedness requires models whose state space and transition rules can change over time, going beyond conventional static formalisms.
status_evidence.claim: Open-ended modelling requires dynamic models/metamodels, which existing static languages do not provide.

status_evidence.title: Open-Endedness in AI and ALife: a survey
status_evidence.snippet: Surveys notions of open-endedness and notes the lack of formal frameworks in which the model itself can evolve as the modelled system evolves.
status_evidence.claim: Constructing dynamic modelling languages and metalanguages for open-ended systems is identified as an outstanding research challenge.
